project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The lignin leaves the mill as wet cake and no lignin dryer is available, so buyers needing dry powder require drying outside the current infrastructure.
The stream is currently fired in the mill's boilers as internal fuel, so diversion to sales would affect the existing fuel route.
Solvent or membrane fractionation and chemical modification are not available at the mill.
Covered cake storage is limited to 1500.0 t wet, constraining wet-cake inventory and staging.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing, limiting pathway and buyer-specification screening.
Moisture is uncertain and affects dry tonnage and shipped mass.
data_quality_notes: The record is marked fictional_demo; the mill, stream, and all figures are illustrative assumptions rather than measurements.
The validated dry-matter balance and composition check passed; the reported composition total is 96.5% of dry matter.
Lignin content has a method_unclear data gap, so comparisons with buyer specifications require confirmation of the analytical method.
Moisture has an uncertainty data gap; shift-level measurements over at least one month are needed before relying on the value.
Missing molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl, and sodium measurements prevent complete pathway qualification.
agent.summary: Validated fictional profile: 40000.0 t/yr wet kraft lignin cake at a moisture fraction of 0.35000000000000003, corresponding to 26000.0 t/yr dry mass; no contradictions were reported, but key composition data are missing and the stream is currently used as internal fuel.

lignin_pct.method: Acid-insoluble (Klason) plus acid-soluble lignin, as % of dry matter (method stated for illustration)

sulfur_pct.method: Total sulfur by elemental analysis (stated for illustration)

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

checks.detail: recorded dry matter 26,000 t/yr; wet quantity x (1 - moisture) = 26,000 t/yr
lignin + ash + carbohydrates = 96.5% of dry matter

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of molecular weight distribution, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of hydroxyl group content, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.
data_gaps.next_step: Log cake moisture for each shift over at least one month.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins used for plywood and other wood-based panels.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin has been reported as industrially proven for veneer plywood and can meet Bonding Class 3.
Published studies report phenol replacement levels up to 50% with depolymerized lignin and up to 80% in a vendor's LPF resin claim.

target_customers.statement: Potential customer types are plywood manufacturers and producers of wood-based panels that use phenol-formaldehyde adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is phenol used in phenol-formaldehyde resins.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
A demonstrated veneer-plywood application met EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3.
The cited laboratory formulation assessed viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard.

limitations: The evidence mixes review findings, vendor technical literature, and a laboratory plywood study.
The reported TRL 8 applies to biobased phenolic resins generally, not specifically to kraft lignin.
The vendor performance and cost claims are not supported by a cited independent test report.
The depolymerized-lignin molecular-weight range is not a specification for lignin as delivered by a mill.
The Pinecrest profile states that chemical modification is unavailable at the mill, while the evidence identifies activation or depolymerization as necessary.
missing_information: No lignin purchase price, annual demand volume, named buyer, contract terms, or regional demand estimate is provided.
No evidence confirms that Pinecrest's wet cake meets the required ash, molecular-weight, or functional-group specifications.
No delivered-product qualification plan or drying responsibility is identified.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents an industrially proven LPF plywood application and substantial product use in wood-panel adhesives, but it does not document commercial sales to established buyers by multiple producers.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Lignin can partially replace petroleum-based polyols in rigid polyurethane and polyisocyanurate insulation foams.

Unmodified kraft lignin has been studied as a partial replacement in flexible polyurethane foam; the evidence suggests kraft lignin may be more suitable for denser, stiffer heavy-duty foams than automotive flexible foam.
The evidence covers polyurethane foams, panels, coatings, and rubber-replacement uses, but rates lignin polyurethane uses at TRL 6 overall.

target_customers.statement: Potential customer types are rigid insulation-foam producers and flexible or heavy-duty polyurethane-foam producers.
Automotive foam producers are an identified application audience, although the evidence says organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is petroleum-based polyol.

qualification_requirements.statement: One study cites total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g, equivalent to 3.56 mmol/g total hydroxyl groups, as an acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production.
In testing, rigid PUR/PIR foams were assessed against ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Kraft lignin generally needs significant treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach target polyurethane properties.

limitations: Most evidence is from laboratory foam studies rather than commercial production.
The rigid-foam pass-rate evidence covers mixed lignin types and does not provide a kraft-only pass rate in the claim.
The cited polyurethane TRL 6 applies to a broad row of uses, not specifically to Pinecrest kraft lignin foam.
A review states that commercialization remains limited by consistency, technical performance, and production cost; the full text was unavailable for that record.
The Pinecrest profile states that chemical modification is unavailable and key molecular-weight and hydroxyl properties are missing.
missing_information: No lignin price, purchase volume, named buyer, contract terms, or regional polyurethane demand estimate is provided.
No evidence establishes that Pinecrest lignin meets the total-hydroxyl threshold or acceptable viscosity and solubility behavior.
No commercial qualification pathway, formulation ownership, or drying and modification responsibility is identified.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows substantial research activity and a broad polyurethane TRL assessment, but it does not document a commercial lignin-based polyurethane buyer, sale, or development partnership.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#3: Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#4: Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.

applications.statement: Lignin can serve as a precursor for carbon fiber, although the evidence identifies demanding purity, spinning, and performance barriers.

Kraft lignin can be used to produce hard carbon for sodium-ion battery anodes; the evidence reports higher initial coulombic efficiency for hard carbon made from kraft lignin than from sulfonated lignin in the cited comparison.
Lignin can be converted into activated carbon, including when its quality is too impure for other carbon-material applications.
A lignin-based anode-material pilot line and planned standardized manufacturing units are documented for lithium-ion battery applications.

target_customers.statement: Potential customer types are carbon-fiber precursor and carbon-fiber manufacturers.
Potential customer types include sodium-ion and lithium-ion battery anode-material manufacturers.
Activated-carbon producers are a potential customer type because the evidence evaluates lignin as an activated-carbon precursor.

competing_materials.statement: Carbon-fiber competition includes PAN-based carbon fiber.
Hard-carbon competition includes fossil precursors such as anthracite and pitch.
Activated carbon made from conventional precursors is an incumbent or competing material.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited carbon-fiber precursor specification requires lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, and removal of particulates larger than 1 micrometre.
The examined kraft lignin needed purification before carbon-fiber use, and softwood lignin requires a plasticizing agent for melt spinning.
Battery-material qualification can take 3 years with battery manufacturers and carmakers, according to the cited company material.

limitations: The carbon-fiber precursor specifications are cited secondhand and come from a study of lignin from a near-neutral hemicellulose extraction process rather than standard kraft pulping.
The carbon-fiber evidence includes older FY2009 work, modelled costs, and a project summary rather than independently verified commercial performance.
The hard-carbon evidence is a review and covers sodium-ion batteries only in the cited record.
The lithium-ion pilot-line evidence is company investor material with forward-looking statements, and its later status was not verified.
The Pinecrest profile has missing composition and sodium data, and wet cake would require additional handling or drying for buyers requiring dry material.
missing_information: No lignin purchase price, annual demand volume, named buyer, contract terms, or regional demand estimate is provided.
No evidence shows that Pinecrest cake meets carbon-fiber purity, ash, volatile, carbohydrate, particulate, or melt-spinning specifications.
No battery-cell performance data, customer acceptance result, or current status of the cited pilot and scale-up plans is provided.
No pathway-specific commercial specification is provided for activated carbon beyond the statement that precursor quality has no strict limitations.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents an industrially relevant precursor-production project, a pilot production line, and qualification activity with battery manufacturers and carmakers, but it does not document established commercial sales to buyers.

processing_requirements.statement: The cake would need activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
A commercial route would require an external or newly installed treatment step because chemical modification is not available at the mill.
Drying would be needed if the buyer requires dry powder, because the material leaves as wet cake and the mill has no lignin dryer.

The product would need customer qualification covering resin viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde, with a demonstrated veneer-plywood formulation meeting Bonding Class 3 as one available benchmark.

technical_maturity.statement: The lignin-plus-phenol-substitution resin route is reported at TRL 9.

adoption_barriers.statement: Plywood and panel customers would need to qualify a lignin-containing adhesive against incumbent phenol-based formulations.
Pinecrest has not demonstrated that its wet cake meets buyer-relevant ash, molecular-weight, or functional-group specifications.
The route competes with phenol and has no identified buyer, purchase terms, demand volume, or drying responsibility.
Diversion from the mill boiler fuel route and limited covered wet-cake storage could complicate supply continuity and staging.

missing_inputs: Pinecrest ash, molecular-weight, and functional-group data
the value and operational impact of replacing the existing boiler-fuel route
assumptions: The deterministic scenario analysis used dry feedstock of 26000.0 t/yr, with conservative and optimistic dry-mass outputs of 21600.0 and 30100.0 t/yr.

The deterministic scenario analysis used wet feedstock assumptions of 36000.0 / 40000.0 / 43000.0 t/yr, moisture assumptions of 40.0 / 35.0 / 30.0 %, and availability fractions of 40.0 / 50.0 / 60.0 % for conservative / base / optimistic cases; these are fictional assumptions.
No default product yield, product price, or variable cost was assumed.
Commercial supply would require an external partner or new assets for activation/depolymerization and potentially drying.
The route would be evaluated initially as a partial phenol substitute rather than as a claim that all phenol is replaced.
uncertainties: Feedstock compatibility could not receive a numeric score because the evidence library provides no numeric phenolic-resin requirements for comparison.
Indicative economics were incomplete: product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, and contribution per tonne were not calculated.
The TRL evidence describes a resin route, but it does not establish that Pinecrest's specific wet cake, treatment route, or customer formulation is ready for sale.
Moisture uncertainty and the existing boiler-fuel use may materially change the practical supply available to customers.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: The pathway is technically mature and has identifiable plywood and panel customers, but Pinecrest would need significant treatment and potentially drying, plus customer qualification and a diversion plan for the existing fuel route. This fits the rubric level of feasibility with significant investment or a partner because the barriers are known.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 9 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-03#1.

indicative_economics.rationale: Gross contribution per tonne could not be calculated. Missing inputs: product yield, product price, variable costs.

report.summary: Carbon materials is the sole ranked pathway at attractiveness 2.19, supported by pilot-level readiness and market activity but weakened by feedstock compatibility score 1 and commercialization-feasibility score 2. Phenolic resins has stronger maturity and indicative attractiveness at 3.73 but remains insufficient data because compatibility and economics are unassessed. Polyurethanes has weaker market evidence and requires modification assets and partners. Validate feedstock properties, buyer-backed specifications and terms, route economics, and boiler-fuel opportunity cost before investment.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
